30-item checklist for investigating a Python HTTP memory leak:

1. Set a baseline and record environment: `python -V && pip freeze | head -50 && ps -p <pid> -o pid,rss,vsz,pcpu,pmem`. Verify env, package versions, and current RSS are captured for comparison.
2. Freeze a known-good repro: script that performs a fixed burst of HTTP requests, e.g. 100–1000 requests with a small concurrency limit. Verify it runs deterministically and produces the symptom.
3. Enable allocations tracing: `import tracemalloc; tracemalloc.start(25)` at app start; snapshot after idle and after load: `snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()`. Verify snapshots exist and include top allocation diffs.
4. Capture RSS/virtual memory over time: `psutil.Process().memory_info().rss` or `/proc/<pid>/status`. Verify RSS trends upward monotonically or jumps correlate with requests.
5. Monitor GC pressure: `gc.get_count()`, `gc.get_stats()`, and periodic `gc.collect()` diffs. Verify whether objects persist across GC or are in unreachable cycles.
6. Use `memory_profiler` or `line_profiler` on request path: `@profile`/`mprof`/`kernprof` around the endpoint handler. Verify hot lines allocate disproportionately or retain objects.
7. Inspect frames with `objgraph`/`pympler` for large objects: `objgraph.show_growth()` or `show_most_common_types()`. Verify whether HTTP response bodies, headers, sessions, or sockets dominate.
8. Check client session/connection reuse: confirm `requests.Session`, `httpx.Client`, `urllib3` pools, or aiohttp `ClientSession` are created once, not per request. Verify a singleton/app-scoped client and no unclosed sessions.
9. Verify response bodies are fully read and closed: always consume `.text`/`.content` or use context managers (`with session.get(...) as r: ...`). Verify no open responses remain and connection pools return sockets.
10. Disable/limit keep-alive and inspect pool settings: `urllib3`/`requests` `pool_maxsize`, `maxsize`, `keepalive`, timeouts. Verify pool size is bounded and sockets are released under reuse.
11. Add timeouts to all HTTP calls: connect/read/total timeouts and total retry budgets. Verify no request can hang forever and retries don’t accumulate responses.
12. Catch and bound retry/backoff behavior: cap retries, dedupe in-flight requests, circuit-break on upstream errors. Verify memory does not grow when upstream is slow/failing.
13. Add request-size guardrails: max response length, streaming caps, content-length checks, and pagination limits. Verify large upstream payloads are rejected/streamed rather than buffered.
14. Stream large downloads instead of buffering: iterate `r.iter_content(chunk_size=...)` and validate chunks. Verify peak RSS stays flat while throughput remains correct.
15. Hunt server-side accumulations: check request logs, in-memory caches, metrics buffers, and queues. Verify no unbounded `list`/`dict` grows per request; add eviction or TTL.
16. Check logging and metrics: request-body/response-body logging, exception traceback retention, label cardinality. Verify logs don’t retain unbounded payloads and metric labels are bounded.

5. Socket state scan — `ss -tnp | grep <PID>` or `netstat -tnp 2>/dev/null | grep <PID>` — Check for many `TIME_WAIT`, `CLOSE_WAIT`, or established connections.
6. Enable GC diagnostics — `python -X importtime -X showrefcount -v -m <app>` or set `PYTHONMALLOC=debug` — Verify allocations occur and GC runs; note unexpected cyclical garbage.

8. Snapshot comparison — capture 3–5 `tracemalloc` snapshots at equal interval after traffic begins, diff top diffs — Confirm growing objects are attributable to request handling.
9. Controlled load generation — use local load tool, e.g. `wrk -t2 -c100 -d60s <local-health-endpoint>` or `hey` — Keep traffic bounded; avoid overwhelming third-party services.
